sangam-literature.name: Sangam literature
sangam-literature.summary: The earliest known literature of South India, composed in classical Tamil, with most scholars dating its historical era to roughly 300 BCE to 300 CE.

k-t-achaya.name: K. T. Achaya
k-t-achaya.summary: Oil chemist, food scientist, nutritionist and food historian (1923–2002), author of works including Indian Food: A Historical Companion.

indo-roman-trade-relations.name: Indo-Roman trade network
indo-roman-trade-relations.summary: Trade between the Indian subcontinent and the Roman Empire, chiefly by a sea route via the Red Sea from around the time of Augustus, exchanging goods such as silk, spices, silver and gold.

avvaiyar-sangam-poet.name: Avvaiyar
avvaiyar-sangam-poet.summary: A Tamil poet of the Sangam period who wrote 59 poems in the Puranaanuru and had cordial relations with the chieftains Vel Pari and Athiyaman; a statue plaque suggests she was born around the 1st century BCE.

chola-dynasty.name: Chola dynasty
chola-dynasty.summary: A Tamil dynasty from southern India that built an expansive maritime empire, reaching its height in the 9th to 13th centuries CE under rulers such as Rajaraja I.

muziris.name: Muziris
muziris.summary: An ancient port on India's Malabar Coast near the Periyar River's mouth, important in the Indian Ocean spice trade with the Middle East and Mediterranean world.

malabar-coast.name: Malabar Coast
malabar-coast.summary: Southwestern coastal region of India stretching from Konkan to Kanyakumari, one of the subcontinent's wettest and most biodiverse areas.

thali.name: Thali
thali.summary: A round platter used across South Asia, Southeast Asia and the Caribbean to serve a full meal made up of several dishes, also used for ceremonial purposes.

tirunelveli.name: Tirunelveli
tirunelveli.summary: A city in Tamil Nadu, India, with a recorded history of over two thousand years, ruled in turn by the Pandyas, Cholas, the Vijayanagara Empire and the British before Indian independence.

rock-cut-architecture.name: Rock-cut architecture
rock-cut-architecture.summary: Creation of buildings and sculptures by excavating solid rock, used for temples, tombs and dwellings; in India this technique began around 250 BCE.

greco-buddhist-art.name: Greco-Buddhist art
greco-buddhist-art.summary: Also called Gandhara art, a style blending Ancient Greek and Buddhist art that flowered under the Kushan Empire and produced the first known depictions of the Buddha in human form.

the-buddha.name: The Buddha
the-buddha.summary: A wandering religious teacher of the 6th or 5th century BCE in the Indo-Gangetic Plain who founded Buddhism, teaching the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path after attaining enlightenment at Bodh Gaya.

kushan-empire.name: Kushan Empire
kushan-empire.summary: A syncretic empire (c. 30–375 CE) formed by the Yuezhi, spreading from Bactria across what is now Afghanistan, Pakistan and northern India; its rulers patronized Buddhism and helped spread it into Central Asia and China.

aniconism-in-buddhism.name: Aniconism
aniconism-in-buddhism.summary: The early Buddhist practice, lasting until the 1st century CE, of showing the Buddha only through symbols such as an empty throne, a riderless horse, or footprints rather than a human figure.

ajanta-caves.name: Ajanta Caves
ajanta-caves.summary: Thirty rock-cut Buddhist cave monuments in Maharashtra, India, dating from the 2nd century BCE to about 480 CE, celebrated for their masterful paintings and sculpture.

barabar-caves.name: Barabar Caves
barabar-caves.summary: The oldest surviving rock-cut caves in India, dating from the Maurya Empire (322-185 BCE) in Bihar, some bearing inscriptions from Emperor Ashoka's reign.

ashoka.name: Ashoka
ashoka.summary: Emperor of the Mauryan dynasty from about 268 BCE, whose empire covered much of the Indian subcontinent; after conquering Kalinga he turned to promoting Buddhism across Asia.

sanchi-stupa.name: Sanchi Stupa
sanchi-stupa.summary: One of the oldest stone structures in India, commissioned by the Mauryan emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE to house relics of the Buddha, later enlarged with carved gateways.

bharhut.name: Bharhut
bharhut.summary: A village in central India known for a Buddhist stupa whose sculptures, dated to around 125 to 75 BCE, are among the earliest examples of Indian and Buddhist art.

bodh-gaya.name: Bodh Gaya
bodh-gaya.summary: A pilgrimage site in Bihar, India, where Gautama Buddha is said to have attained enlightenment under the Bodhi Tree; in Buddhist use since the Maurya period.

amaravati-stupa.name: Amaravati Stupa
amaravati-stupa.summary: A ruined Buddhist stupa in Andhra Pradesh, India, built in phases from the third century BCE to about 250 CE, its sculptures now regarded as one of ancient India's three major art styles.

shunga-empire.name: Shunga Empire
shunga-empire.summary: Ruling entity centred on Magadha that controlled most of northern India from about 187 to 75 BCE, founded by Pushyamitra after he took the Mauryan throne.

pataliputra-capital.name: Pataliputra capital
pataliputra-capital.summary: A monumental stone capital with volutes and Classical Greek designs from the 3rd century BCE, found at the Mauryan capital Pataliputra.

karla-caves.name: Karla Caves
karla-caves.summary: A complex of ancient Buddhist rock-cut caves near Lonavala, India, developed from the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE, known for the well-preserved 'Grand Chaitya' hall.

masarh-lion.name: Masarh lion
masarh-lion.summary: A stone sculpture found near Arrah in the Indian state of Bihar, generally dated to the 3rd century BCE.

pataliputra.name: Pataliputra
pataliputra.summary: An ancient Indian city near modern Patna, capital of major powers including the Maurya and Gupta empires, and one of the largest cities in the world under the Mauryas.

chunar.name: Chunar
chunar.summary: A city in Mirzapur district, Uttar Pradesh, India, known for its historic Chunar Fort and for handicrafts made of clay and plaster of paris.

pillars-of-ashoka.name: Pillars of Ashoka
pillars-of-ashoka.summary: Monolithic stone columns erected across the Indian subcontinent by Mauryan emperor Ashoka (c. 268–232 BC), inscribed with his edicts; twenty still survive today.

swaraj-prakash-gupta.name: S. P. Gupta
swaraj-prakash-gupta.summary: Indian archaeologist and art historian (1931–2007) known for excavations of Indus Valley Civilisation sites and for directing the Allahabad Museum.

alexander-cunningham.name: Alexander Cunningham
alexander-cunningham.summary: A British Army engineer (1814-1893) who became fascinated by Indian history and archaeology, founding what became the Archaeological Survey of India and amassing major artefact collections.

kharosthi.name: Kharosthi Script
kharosthi.summary: An ancient Indic writing system developed in the Gandhara region between the 5th and 3rd centuries BCE, used along the Silk Road until dying out around the 5th century CE.

kalinga-war.name: Kalinga War
kalinga-war.summary: A war around 261 BCE on India's east coast, in what is now Odisha, that marked the end of Ashoka's military conquests after the Mauryan founder Chandragupta Maurya.

kalinga-region.name: Kalinga
kalinga-region.summary: A historical region of eastern coastal India between the Ganges and Godavari rivers, roughly matching modern Odisha, ruled by many regional dynasties over the centuries.

alexander-the-great.name: Alexander the Great
alexander-the-great.summary: King of Macedon from 336 BC who conquered much of the known world by age 30, creating an empire stretching from Greece to India; tutored by Aristotle.

porus.name: Porus
porus.summary: An ancient Indian king (fl. 326–321 BC) who fought Alexander the Great at the Battle of the Hydaspes and was reinstated, with expanded territory, as Alexander's satrap.

pauravas.name: Pauravas
pauravas.summary: An ancient tribe of the northern Indus valley to which Raja Porus is thought to have belonged.

jhelum-river.name: Jhelum River (Hydaspes)
jhelum-river.summary: The westernmost of the Punjab region's five major rivers, flowing about 725 km from Indian-administered Kashmir through Pakistan to join the Chenab River.

mahabharata.name: Mahabharata
mahabharata.summary: One of the two great Sanskrit epics of ancient India, centred on the Kurukshetra War between royal cousins and containing the Bhagavad Gita, compiled mostly between the 3rd century BCE and 3rd century CE.

darius-iii.name: Darius III
darius-iii.summary: Last Achaemenid King of Persia (336–330 BC), defeated by Alexander the Great in several battles before being killed by his own relative Bessus.

battle-of-gaugamela.name: Battle of Gaugamela
battle-of-gaugamela.summary: The decisive 331 BC battle in which Alexander the Great's outnumbered army defeated Darius III's Persian forces, effectively ending the Achaemenid Empire.

nanda-empire.name: Nanda Empire
nanda-empire.summary: A powerful 4th-century BCE empire based in Magadha, northeastern India, noted for great wealth and a large army; its last king was overthrown by Chandragupta Maurya.

magadha.name: Magadha
magadha.summary: Ancient Indian kingdom in the eastern Ganges Plain that formed the core of major dynasties including the Mauryan and Gupta empires, and played a key role in the development of Buddhism and Jainism.

beas-river.name: Hyphasis River
beas-river.summary: The ancient Greek name for the Beas River in northwestern India, where Alexander the Great's exhausted army mutinied and refused to march further east.

chanakya.name: Chanakya
chanakya.summary: A Brahmin traditionally said to have helped Chandragupta Maurya found the Maurya Empire and served as chief adviser to him and his son; conventionally, though now doubtfully, identified as the political writer Kautilya.

arthashastra.name: Arthashastra
arthashastra.summary: An ancient Indian Sanskrit treatise on statecraft, politics, economic policy and military strategy, traditionally linked to the minister Kautilya.

chandragupta-maurya.name: Chandragupta Maurya
chandragupta-maurya.summary: Founder and first emperor of the Maurya Empire, who overthrew the Nanda dynasty around 320 BCE and later resisted the Greeks to take control of the eastern Indus Valley.

craterus.name: Craterus
craterus.summary: Macedonian general (c. 370–321 BC) who served loyally under Alexander the Great, commanding troops at battles including Issus and the Hydaspes, and later became one of the Diadochi who divided Alexander's empire.

seleucid-mauryan-war.name: Seleucid–Mauryan War
seleucid-mauryan-war.summary: A conflict around 305 to 303 BCE between Seleucus I's Seleucid Empire and Chandragupta Maurya's Mauryan Empire, ending in a peace treaty, a marriage alliance, and 500 war elephants given to Seleucus.

battle-of-ipsus.name: Battle of Ipsus
battle-of-ipsus.summary: A 301 BC battle among Alexander the Great's successors in which a coalition led by Lysimachus, Cassander and Seleucus I defeated Antigonus I Monophthalmus and his son Demetrius.

megasthenes.name: Megasthenes
megasthenes.summary: Greek historian and diplomat (died c. 290 BCE) who wrote Indica, the first written Western account of India, based on his time at the Mauryan court.

dilip-kumar-chakrabarti.name: Dilip K. Chakrabarti
dilip-kumar-chakrabarti.summary: Indian archaeologist, born 1941, Professor Emeritus of South Asian Archaeology at Cambridge University, known for research on early iron use in India and the archaeology of eastern India.

samudragupta.name: Samudragupta
samudragupta.summary: Second emperor of the Gupta Empire of ancient India, who ruled from 318 to 375 and greatly expanded its territory through military campaigns.

gedrosia.name: Gedrosia
gedrosia.summary: An ancient Persian province in the coastal Makran region (roughly modern Balochistan), stretching from the Indus River to near the Strait of Hormuz.

makran.name: Makran
makran.summary: Semi-desert coastal region of Balochistan along the Gulf of Oman, split between Pakistan and Iran.

kamil-zvelebil.name: Kamil Zvelebil
kamil-zvelebil.summary: A Czech scholar (1927–2009) of Indian literature and linguistics, especially Tamil, Sanskrit, and Dravidian studies.

bharatas-vedic-tribe.name: Bharatas
bharatas-vedic-tribe.summary: An early Vedic tribe from the second millennium BCE whose king Sudās won the Battle of the Ten Kings, after which its people helped form the Kuru kingdom, India's first attested state.

pali-canon.name: Pāli Canon
pali-canon.summary: The standard collection of Theravada Buddhist scriptures in the Pali language, first recited orally after the Buddha's death and not written down until about 29 BCE.

gupta-script.name: Gupta script
gupta-script.summary: A writing system used for Sanskrit during the Gupta Empire, descended from the Brahmi script and ancestor of the Nagari, Sarada and Siddham scripts.

brahmi-script.name: Brahmi script
brahmi-script.summary: An ancient Indian writing system, fully developed by the 3rd century BCE, whose descendants are still used across South and Southeast Asia; deciphered by James Prinsep in the 1830s.

n-gar-script.name: Nagari script
n-gar-script.summary: An ancestor of the Devanagari script, first used for Prakrit and Sanskrit, in regular use by the 7th century CE and descended from the ancient Brahmi script family.

sharada-script.name: Sharada script
sharada-script.summary: An abugida script of the Brahmic family used between the 8th and 12th centuries in Kashmir and nearby regions to write Sanskrit and Kashmiri; now rarely used outside religious contexts.

siddha-script.name: Siddham script
siddha-script.summary: Medieval Indic script used in India from the 6th to 13th century, derived from the Gupta script and ancestral to Nāgarī; still used by East Asian Buddhists for writing mantras.

madurai.name: Madurai
madurai.summary: Major city in Tamil Nadu, India, on the Vaigai River, one of the oldest cities in South Asia with a documented history of more than 2,500 years.

tolk-ppiyam.name: Tolkāppiyam
tolk-ppiyam.summary: The oldest surviving Tamil grammar text and the oldest extant work of Tamil literature, covering phonology, morphology, and poetics; dated as early as the 2nd century BCE by some scholars.

eight-anthologies.name: Eight Anthologies
eight-anthologies.summary: A classical Tamil poetic work known as the Eight Anthologies, part of the oldest surviving Tamil literature, composed roughly between the 1st century BCE and 5th century CE.

ten-idylls.name: Ten Idylls
ten-idylls.summary: An anthology of ten long poems from early Tamil Sangam literature, composed roughly between the 2nd and 5th centuries CE, including guides for bards and to religious devotion.

ramayana.name: Ramayana
ramayana.summary: An ancient Sanskrit epic poem narrating the life of Rama, one of Hinduism's two major epics, with its oral origins estimated between the 8th and 4th centuries BCE.

numit-kappa.name: Numit Kappa
numit-kappa.summary: An ancient Meitei-language mythological epic, believed written around or before 33 AD, considered the oldest known epic in Meitei literature.

khwai-nongchengpam-piba.name: Khwai Nongchengpam Piba
khwai-nongchengpam-piba.summary: A slave, rebel and archer in the 1st-century Meitei epic Numit Kappa, remembered for shooting down one of two suns, an act that sets the story's events in motion.

meitei-language.name: Meitei
meitei-language.summary: A Tibeto-Burman language of northeast India, the official language of Manipur, with about 1.76 million native speakers.

pallava-dynasty.name: Pallava dynasty
pallava-dynasty.summary: A dynasty ruling parts of southern India from 275 to 897 CE, reaching its height under Mahendravarman I and Narasimhavarman I and known for patronizing Hindu temple architecture and the Pallava script.

pallava-script.name: Pallava script
pallava-script.summary: A script named after the Pallava dynasty of southern India, attested from the 4th century CE, used to write Tamil and Sanskrit and ancestral to scripts such as Khmer, Thai and Javanese.

grantha-script.name: Grantha script
grantha-script.summary: A classical South Indian script used mainly in Tamil Nadu and Kerala, descended from the Pallava script and ancestor of the modern Malayalam script.

khmer-script.name: Khmer script
khmer-script.summary: An abugida script for writing the Khmer language and, in Buddhist liturgy, Pali, written left to right with stacked consonant clusters and both independent and dependent vowel marks.

gandhara.name: Gandhara
gandhara.summary: An ancient Indo-Aryan region centered on the Peshawar valley, in what is now northwest Pakistan and northeast Afghanistan, known as an influential Buddhist civilization.

gandhari-language.name: Gandhari Prakrit
gandhari-language.summary: An Indo-Aryan Prakrit language used from about the 3rd century BCE to the 4th century CE in the Gandhara region, notable for its archaic sounds and its Kharoshthi script.

kumbakonam.name: Kumbakonam
kumbakonam.summary: City in Tamil Nadu, India, known as a "temple city" for its many Hindu shrines, historically ruled by the Cholas, Pandyas and others, and called the "Cambridge of South India" under British rule.

a-vagho-a.name: Aśvaghoṣa
a-vagho-a.summary: A Buddhist philosopher, poet and dramatist from India, c. 80–150 CE, believed to be the first Sanskrit dramatist and among the greatest Indian poets before Kālidāsa.

cilappatikaram.name: Cilappatikaram
cilappatikaram.summary: An ancient Tamil epic poem of 5,730 lines, probably composed in the 5th century CE, telling the tragic love story of Kannaki and her husband Kōvalan.

manimekalai.name: Manimekalai
manimekalai.summary: A Tamil Buddhist epic composed between the 2nd and 6th centuries, telling of a dancer-nun who resists a prince's advances and seeks to free herself from worldly ties.

kartikeya.name: Murugan
kartikeya.summary: A Tamil deity of the Kurinji region, later merged with the Hindu war god Skanda Kartikeya; patron deity of the Tamil language, celebrated in Sangam-era works.

sushruta-samhita.name: Sushruta Samhita
sushruta-samhita.summary: Ancient Sanskrit medical text and a foundational work of Ayurveda, notable for uniquely detailed chapters on surgical training, instruments, and procedures; its oldest surviving manuscript dates to 878 CE.

sushruta.name: Sushruta
sushruta.summary: Ancient Indian physician and surgeon credited with major advances in plastic and cataract surgery, and author of a foundational Ayurvedic medical treatise.

ayurveda.name: Ayurveda
ayurveda.summary: A traditional medicine system from the Indian subcontinent, still widely practiced in India and Nepal, using herbal remedies, diet and ancient surgical techniques.

p-ini.name: Pāṇini
p-ini.summary: An ancient Indian Sanskrit grammarian and linguist of the mid-1st millennium BCE whose work, the Ashtadhyayi, codified Classical Sanskrit and later influenced modern Western linguistics.

charaka-samhita.name: Charaka Samhita
charaka-samhita.summary: An ancient Sanskrit text on Ayurveda attributed to Charaka, one of the two foundational surviving texts of Indian traditional medicine.

atharvaveda.name: Atharvaveda
atharvaveda.summary: The fourth Veda of Hinduism, a collection of about 730 hymns covering everyday rituals, initiation, marriage and funerals alongside its more magical formulas.

maurya-empire.name: Maurya Empire
maurya-empire.summary: A large Iron Age empire in South Asia founded around 320 BCE by Chandragupta Maurya and lasting until 185 BCE, reaching its height under his grandson Ashoka.

gupta-empire.name: Gupta Empire
gupta-empire.summary: An Indian empire from the mid-3rd to mid-6th century CE that ruled much of northern India, a period often called India's Golden Age for its cultural and scientific advances.

yuezhi.name: Yuezhi
yuezhi.summary: An ancient nomadic people from Gansu whose defeat by the Xiongnu in 176 BC set off migrations that eventually produced the Kushan Empire.

dhana-nanda.name: Dhana Nanda
dhana-nanda.summary: The last Nanda king of Magadha, defeated by Chandragupta Maurya around 321 BCE, an event that ended the Nanda Empire and began the Maurya Empire.

seleucus-i-nicator.name: Seleucus I Nicator
seleucus-i-nicator.summary: A Macedonian Greek general under Alexander the Great (c. 358–281 BC) who later founded the Seleucid Empire, eventually ruling Asia Minor, Syria, Mesopotamia and the Iranian plateau.

seleucid-empire.name: Seleucid Empire
seleucid-empire.summary: A Greek state in West Asia founded by Seleucus I Nicator in 312 BC after Alexander the Great's empire divided, ruling from Seleucia and Antioch until Rome annexed it in 63 BC.

bindusara.name: Bindusara
bindusara.summary: The second Mauryan emperor of Magadha in ancient India, ruling about 297–273 BCE; son of the dynasty's founder Chandragupta and father of its most famous ruler, Ashoka.

pandya-dynasty.name: Pandya dynasty
pandya-dynasty.summary: An ancient Tamil dynasty of South India, one of the three great Tamil kingdoms, ruling with varying extent from about 400 BCE to 1618 CE.

vedic-period.name: Vedic period
vedic-period.summary: A period in India's late Bronze and early Iron Age, roughly 1500 to 500 BCE, when the Vedas were composed by Indo-Aryan tribes who had migrated into the northwestern subcontinent.

varna-hinduism.name: varna system
varna-hinduism.summary: A fourfold Hindu social classification—Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras—described in Brahmanical texts and traced back to the Rigveda.

j-ti.name: Jāti
j-ti.summary: Traditional term for a cohesive group in Indian society, like a caste, sub-caste, clan or tribe, often tied to occupation, geography, language or religious belief.

edicts-of-ashoka.name: Edicts of Ashoka
edicts-of-ashoka.summary: Over thirty inscriptions on pillars, boulders and cave walls by Mauryan emperor Ashoka (268-232 BCE), the earliest datable written texts from India, setting out his policy of nonviolence and tolerance.

kanva-dynasty.name: Kanva dynasty
kanva-dynasty.summary: A ruling dynasty of Magadha in eastern India that lasted from 73 to 28 BCE, after its founder overthrew the preceding Shunga dynasty.

faxian.name: Faxian
faxian.summary: A Chinese Buddhist monk who traveled overland to India starting around age 60 to collect Buddhist scriptures, journeying from 399 to 412 CE and writing an early account of Buddhist India.

chandragupta-ii.name: Chandragupta II
chandragupta-ii.summary: Emperor of the Gupta Empire from about 375 to 415 CE, who expanded it to its greatest extent and whose court hosted celebrated scholars known as the Navaratnas.

nyaya.name: Nyaya
nyaya.summary: One of six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy, whose name means 'justice' or 'method,' known for its systematic theories of logic and epistemology.

vaisheshika.name: Vaisheshika
vaisheshika.summary: One of the six classical schools of Hindu philosophy from ancient India, known for developing an atomist theory of the physical universe.

samkhya.name: Samkhya
samkhya.summary: A dualistic school of Hindu philosophy holding that reality consists of two principles: consciousness (Purusha) and matter or nature (Prakriti).

m-m-s.name: Mīmāṃsā
m-m-s.summary: One of six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy, focused on interpreting Vedic ritual texts; it later influenced the Vedānta tradition.

charvaka.name: Charvaka
charvaka.summary: An ancient Indian school of philosophical materialism that rejected ritualism, relied on direct perception, and developed during the first millennium BCE.

pyrrho.name: Pyrrho
pyrrho.summary: Greek philosopher (c. 360–270 BC) from Elis, considered the first Greek skeptic and founder of the school of thought later called Pyrrhonism.

pyrrhonism.name: Pyrrhonism
pyrrhonism.summary: An Ancient Greek school of philosophical skepticism founded by Aenesidemus in the 1st century BCE, inspired by Pyrrho and Timon of Phlius, urging suspension of judgment on all beliefs.

diogenes-laertius.name: Diogenes Laërtius
diogenes-laertius.summary: Biographer of the Greek philosophers (3rd century CE) whose surviving work, Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers, is a key source for ancient Greek philosophy.

three-marks-of-existence.name: Three marks of existence
three-marks-of-existence.summary: A core Buddhist teaching describing three qualities of all existence: impermanence, suffering, and the absence of a lasting self.

upanishads.name: Upanishads
upanishads.summary: Sanskrit texts of the late Vedic period marking a shift from Vedic ritual toward meditation and philosophy, and central to Hinduism's concepts of Atman and Brahman.

moksha.name: Moksha
moksha.summary: A term in Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism for liberation from the cycle of death and rebirth, seen in Hindu tradition as the ultimate aim of human life.

vedas.name: Vedas
vedas.summary: A large body of ancient Indian religious texts and the oldest layer of Sanskrit literature, orally transmitted since the 2nd millennium BCE and regarded as the oldest scriptures of Hinduism.

vedanta.name: Vedanta
vedanta.summary: One of the six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy, meaning 'conclusion of the Vedas,' interpreting the Upanishads, Brahma Sutras and Bhagavad Gita through many later traditions.

mahavira.name: Mahavira
mahavira.summary: Indian religious reformer regarded by Jains as the 24th and final Tirthankara, believed to have lived in the 6th or 5th century BCE; he renounced worldly life around age 30 and preached for 30 years after attaining omniscience.

ny-ya-s-tras.name: Nyāya Sūtras
ny-ya-s-tras.summary: The foundational text of the Nyaya school of Hindu philosophy, containing 528 aphoristic sutras on reason, logic, epistemology and metaphysics across five books.

ahimsa.name: Ahimsa
ahimsa.summary: The ancient Indian principle of nonviolence toward all living beings, a core virtue in Jainism, Buddhism, and Hinduism, later popularized by Mohandas Gandhi.

chandogya-upanishad.name: Chandogya Upanishad
chandogya-upanishad.summary: An ancient Sanskrit text within the Sama Veda, composed roughly between the 8th and 6th centuries BCE, exploring speech, ritual and metaphysical questions, including the teaching 'that('s how) you are.'

rama-a.name: Śramaṇa tradition
rama-a.summary: A broad tradition of wandering ascetics in ancient India, developing alongside but separate from the Vedic religion, that included Jainism, Buddhism and other movements rejecting Vedic authority.

p-r-van-tha.name: Parshvanatha
p-r-van-tha.summary: The 23rd of 24 tirthankaras of Jainism and its earliest tirthankara acknowledged as historical, living around the 9th to 7th century BCE and founding a proto-Jain ascetic community later revived by Mahavira.

tirthankara.name: Tirthankara
tirthankara.summary: In Jainism, a supreme teacher who has conquered the cycle of rebirth and shows others the path to liberation; 24 are said to appear in each half-cycle of time, the last being Mahavira.

kural.name: Kural
kural.summary: Classic Tamil text of 1,330 couplets on virtue, wealth and love, traditionally attributed to Valluvar and dated between 300 BCE and 500 CE, praised as the "Tamil Veda".

thiruvalluvar.name: Valluvar
thiruvalluvar.summary: An Indian Tamil poet and philosopher best known for the Tirukkuṟaḷ, a collection of couplets on ethics, politics and love, though little is known for certain about his life or exact dates.

brahma-sutras.name: Brahma Sutras
brahma-sutras.summary: A Sanskrit text attributed to the sage Badarayana, completed in its surviving form around 400–450 CE, synthesizing Upanishadic ideas around Brahman as the sole origin of existence.

yoga-philosophy.name: Yoga philosophy
yoga-philosophy.summary: One of the six major schools of Hindu philosophy, built on a dualism between consciousness (Puruṣa) and nature (Prakṛti), aiming at liberation through insight and self-restraint.

indo-aryan-peoples.name: Indo-Aryan peoples
indo-aryan-peoples.summary: A diverse group of peoples across South Asia who traditionally speak Indo-Aryan languages, descended from Indo-Iranian pastoralists who migrated from Central Asia.

mark-w-muesse.name: Mark W. Muesse
mark-w-muesse.summary: American philosopher, theologian and teacher, born 1957.

tman-hinduism.name: Ātman
tman-hinduism.summary: In Hinduism, the eternal, unchanging innermost essence or self of a living being, often translated as soul but better understood as "Self."

brahman.name: Brahman
brahman.summary: In Hindu philosophy, the ultimate reality from which all existence proceeds and to which it returns, described as the unchanging foundation of the universe.

stika-and-n-stika.name: Āstika and nāstika
stika-and-n-stika.summary: Terms scholars use to classify schools of Indian philosophy: āstika schools accept the Vedas as authoritative, while nāstika schools do not.

romila-thapar.name: Romila Thapar
romila-thapar.summary: Indian historian born in 1931 and a leading scholar of ancient India, known for social-historical analysis of Vedic-era society and works such as Early India: From Origins to AD 1300.

m-n-srinivas.name: M. N. Srinivas
m-n-srinivas.summary: Indian sociologist and social anthropologist, 1916 to 1999, known for pioneering work on caste, social stratification and Sanskritisation in southern India.
